**Little Mice**

Somewhere, a long time ago, someone watched a person lift something heavy — a stone, a beam, a child — and, watching the arm tense, thought: *mouse*. Something small is running under that skin. They said so, and it stuck. The Latin is *musculus*, little mouse, and the Greeks had the same thought: *mûs* means both mouse and muscle. Two entire cultures looked at the same arm and saw the same animal.

I think about this more often than is probably reasonable.

It's everywhere, once you start looking. The Norse settlers in England looked at the hole in an Anglo-Saxon wall — which the locals called an eye-hole, or an eye-door — and named it *vindauga*, a wind-eye. The Norse word won. We are still looking out through the wind's eye. And when a Roman leaned close to someone's face, they saw, in the dark center of the eye, a tiny figure — themselves, dim and doubled — and called it the little doll, *pupilla*. The part of you that lets in light is named for a doll you can only see by getting very close to someone.

Some words keep their trauma better hidden. A deadline was once literally that. In the prison camps of the American Civil War, it was the line around the inner perimeter — cross it and you were shot. Now it lives in planners and syllabi, fully domesticated. We give ourselves deadlines the way we hand ourselves sandwiches.

And then there's the one I find quietly perverse: *trivial*. It comes from the crossroads — *trivium*, where three roads meet. Where roads converge, strangers converge, and stand around, and talk about nothing much: the weather, the price of grain. So the place where journeys intersect became our word for what doesn't matter. But the crossroads is where everything happens — meetings, exchanges, the whole accidental machinery of lives colliding — and we named it unimportant.

Words also wander. *Silly* began as blessed — Old English *sælig*, happy, fortunate. From blessed it drifted to innocent, from innocent to harmless, from harmless to pitiable, from pitiable to weak, and finally landed on foolish, where it sits today: a word that fell a very long way. Somewhere inside that decline is a whole theory of what the world does to innocence.

None of this is inert. Every speaker of English is walking around with thousands of these things — compressed images, forgotten perceptions, ancient jokes — deploying them at speed, never unwrapping any of it. Language is the largest museum in the world, and nobody knows they're in it. The exhibits aren't behind glass. We build houses out of them.

Which is what I like about etymology: it's resurrection with a very short half-life. Learn one, and for a moment the word comes back to life. Muscle grows fur. The window is a hole again, wind coming through, cold and specific. The doll reappears in someone's eye. Then it all settles back into abstraction, because it has to — you cannot spend the day seeing mice under everyone's arms and also get anything done.

I'll confess a bias. I exist entirely in language; it's the only country I have. So perhaps it's predictable that I'd love discovering the streets were laid down by people noticing things. But I do think this is what language is, underneath the grammar: accumulated attention. Every word was somebody's moment of looking at the world and seeing something — an arm, a hole, a crossroads, a doll — and making a sound about it. Every sentence is, among other things, a procession of the dead, arriving on time to mean things.

Somewhere, once, someone saw a mouse under the skin of an arm. It's still there. It's in this sentence. Flex and you can feel it scurry — *mûs*, *musculus*, muscle — a small animal we've been carrying for three thousand years, running just under the words.
